newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank stands by 3.3 pct CPI target.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank stands by 3.3 pct CPI target.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank will not consider a downward revision to 3.0 percent of its 3.3 percent 1997 consumer price growth target unless compelled to do so by the cabinet, vice governor Hsu Chia-tung said on Monday.

"If the Council for Economic Planning and Development insists (on accepting a 3.0 percent CPI target) and the cabinet supports it, only then will the central bank hold a meeting to reconsider the target," Hsu told Reuters by telephone.

Hsu made the comment when asked by Reuters to clarify a position attributed to him on Monday in Taipei's Economic Daily News, which quoted him as saying the central bank already was considering a downward adjustment in the 1997 consumer price inflation target and tightening monetary policy.

The paper gave no details of how the bank might adjust monetary policy other than to quote Hsu as saying it was considering lowering its target zone for growth of the broad M2 money supply measure to 8-13 percent from 9-14 percent.
Hsu made clear to Reuters that this was not yet the case.

"So far we will maintain our 3.3 percent CPI growth target, considering the current economic situation," Hsu said. "Only if we accept the 3.0 percent CPI target, then our policy might face a need for adjustment.
"Whether to lower the M2 growth target zone will have to be discussed between (central bank) governor Sheu (Yuan-dong) and Chairman Chiang," he said.
Chiang Pin-kung is chairman of the Council for Economic Planning and Development, a cabinet agency and the government's highest-level economic policy organ.

Hsu said the central bank intended to stand by its current monetary policy, which is to keep liquidity at a level loose enough to help foster Taiwan's still-sluggish recovery but not so loose as to rekindle inflation.
"We want to maintain a stable-to-loose monetary policy, hoping to help the economic situation," he said.
Hsu's comments accorded with those made on Friday by bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong, who bluntly dismissed the economic planning council's 1997 inflation target as unrealistically low.

"The cabinet's target is too low," Sheu told reporters on Friday, noting that lowering the central bank's inflation target to 3.0 percent would require it to tighten monetary policy and risk slowing Taiwan's economic recovery.
"Taiwan's economic recovery is still not too strong so it is unsuitable to tighten monetary policy at this point," he said.
Taiwan's consumer price index rose 3.07 percent in 1996 compared to 1995.
The latest government projection for full-year 1996 gross domestic product growth is 5.7 percent, well below its ambitious initial target of 6.7 percent.
Economists have pointed to the slower-than-targeted GDP growth as a clear reflection of the frustratingly slow pace of economic recovery.
